stories.title: Baubap generates a credit line of US$23 million to bank more Mexicans
stories.summary: Mexican fintech Baubap secured a $23 million credit line to expand microloans to millions of unbanked Mexicans. Using alternative data from mobile devices, they approve loans under $25 in seconds—and have already served over 2 million people.
stories.extended_summary: Baubap founders Roberto Salcedo and Luis Villarreal knew firsthand that traditional banks reject millions of Mexicans—especially informal workers and those without credit history. So they built risk models using mobile device data, approving microloans from $25 in under 30 seconds. With a new $23 million credit line from BBVA Spark and SixPoint Capital—now entirely in Mexican pesos—they're poised to grow. The company has already granted over 8 million loans to 2 million people, with a revenue run-rate exceeding $100 million and sustained profitability.

stories.title: Meet the A.I. Ph.D. Who Took Human Error Out of the World’s Biggest Games
stories.summary: The man behind Hawk-Eye—the AI system that calls lines in tennis and reviews fouls in World Cup soccer—is Paul Hawkins, a British entrepreneur with a Ph.D. in AI. His invention, born after a bad cricket umpiring decision, now shapes 25 sports worldwide.
stories.extended_summary: During a World Cup match, VAR reviews a penalty—and at its core is Hawk-Eye, the computer vision system that tracks ball and player positions with 16 high-resolution cameras. Its creator, Paul Hawkins, had a Ph.D. in AI and a burning memory of a bad cricket umpiring call. That frustration led him to develop Hawk-Eye in 2001, now used across tennis, soccer, cricket, rugby, and more. Andre Agassi called it 'the biggest thing to happen in tennis for 40 years.' Hawkins proved that one bad call can spark a revolution.

stories.title: RealQuest AI Wants Your Kid's Screen Time to Look Like a Startup, Not a Scroll
stories.summary: A new app called RealQuest AI turns teens' screen time into a business-building game. Created by a dad who was tired of fighting his kids' device addiction, it guides them to start and run real companies with AI help.
stories.extended_summary: Zach Barney, a father of five, couldn't stop his neurodivergent kids from finding ways around screen restrictions. So he built a platform that gamifies building a business: an AI coach walks teens through creating a product, finding customers, and launching a site. It's like Duolingo meets a startup incubator — turning endless scrolling into something productive and even profitable.

stories.title: Spanish Fork Family Builds a Game Studio With AI — and Jobs for Their Sons
stories.summary: When their twin sons on the autism spectrum couldn't find jobs after graduation, a Utah couple built them a video game company. Gotta Play Games launched its debut title in just four months, creating employment for all eight kids.
stories.extended_summary: Parker and Colby Camp applied to job after job with no luck. So their parents, Brandon and Elena, founded Gotta Play Games—a studio run by the whole family. In four months, they went from a kitchen-table card game to a manufactured product with apps, packaging, and a marketing campaign. The debut title, Skip the Salad, is now live, proving that when the job market won't hire your kids, you can build a company that will.

stories.title: Denver cleantech company Actuate wins Colorado Companies to Watch award
stories.summary: Denver cleantech startup Actuate won a Colorado Companies to Watch award for its building intelligence platform that cuts energy costs by 10–30% for small commercial properties. Founded by a team with 50+ years of experience, they're now expanding to convenience stores and retail chains.
stories.extended_summary: Actuate's Act Hub platform uses internet-connected sensors and AI to manage HVAC, refrigeration, and lighting for buildings that lack traditional management systems—think quick-service restaurant franchises and regional retailers. The result? Clients see 10–30% lower energy costs, 20–30% lower maintenance costs, and 40–60% fewer emergency service calls. Co-founder Allison Fitzpatrick says, 'We started Actuate because we saw an enormous, underserved market.' With the Colorado Companies to Watch award and plans to target convenience stores, they're proving that small buildings can have smart systems too.
